paragraphs: This checklist is only for self-questioning. It is not a hiring standard, ability score, evaluation of job competence, or advice about systems, data, or engineering. This page corresponds to U.S. O*NET/SOC 15-1299.02, Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians (the fixed Chinese index name translates as Information Systems Technologists and Technicians; common recruitment and industry titles include GIS analyst, GIS technician, GIS administrator, GIS coordinator, GIS developer, and geospatial technician). The official scope is assisting scientists or related professionals in building, maintaining, modifying, or using GIS databases, with some custom application development or user support also possible. O*NET core tasks include reviewing existing or incoming data for currency, accuracy, usefulness, quality, and documentation completeness (importance 82); producing data layers, maps, tables, or reports using spatial analysis procedures or GIS technology, equipment, and systems (81); maintaining or modifying existing GIS databases (78); selecting cartographic elements needed to present information effectively (71); entering data into GIS databases through coordinate geometry, keyboard entry of tabular data, manual digitizing, scanning, or automatic vectorization (68); interpreting aerial or orthophoto imagery (67); using specialized application software to create, analyze, report, convert, and transfer data (66); designing, programming, or modeling GIS applications or procedures (64); building, modeling, or analyzing geospatial data using advanced spatial analysis, data manipulation, or cartographic software (64); meeting clients to discuss technical specifications, custom solutions, or operational issues (63); designing and preparing graphical representations of GIS data (63); providing GIS technical expertise to clients or users (63); designing or coordinating development of integrated spatial or nonspatial GIS databases (62); discussing with users to analyze, configure, or troubleshoot applications (61); gathering, compiling, or integrating GIS data, including remote sensing or cartographic data, for map manuscripts (59); converting or rescaling raw imagery information onto maps or other imagery (59); performing integrated or computerized GIS analysis to solve scientific problems (58); providing users or clients technical support for maintenance, development, or operation of GIS databases, equipment, or applications (58); conducting research, data analysis, system design, or support for GIS or GPS mapping software (58); keeping up with GIS technology, equipment, and systems through current literature, peer exchanges, continuing education, or professional organizations and conferences (57); writing, designing, coding, or testing GIS models, internet mapping solutions, or other applications (57); creating geospatial visualizations using complex procedures such as analytical modeling, three-dimensional rendering, or cartographic output (54); and recommending process, equipment, or software upgrades to improve data accessibility or usability (51). Work features environmentally controlled indoor settings (89% daily), prolonged sitting (78% continually or almost continually), the importance of being exact or highly accurate (69% extremely important and 27% very important), email (35% daily), and varying autonomy (for priorities, 34% a lot of freedom, 32% limited freedom, and 20% very little freedom). O*NET details show the 2024 industry distribution for parent group 15-1299: professional, scientific, and technical services 27%, government 23%, and other industries, including information and finance and insurance, 50%. The 50% is a category in the original table; the three categories total 100%. This is neither a separate GIS distribution nor 2025 data.

Exercise instructions | Use the six G1 materials M1—M6 below. In 60 minutes, using only paper, a pen, and a calculator, independently create calculation, discrepancy/quality check, and handover tables. The exercise provides coordinates in meters/degrees, unique keys, population figures, a 500m boundary-inclusive criterion, a 1:10000 scale, an erroneous v2 draft, and Q/T times. The answers show each calculation; no external templates/data or mandatory expert are needed.

Work context shows environmentally controlled indoor work: 89% daily; prolonged sitting: 78% continually or almost continually; importance of being exact or highly accurate: 69% extremely important and 27% very important; determining tasks, priorities, and goals: 34% a lot of freedom; email: 35% daily; repeating the same tasks: 27% extremely important; telephone communication: 47% weekly or more but not daily; and face-to-face or individual and team discussions: 33% daily and 40% weekly or more but not daily. If you are willing to work with geospatial data, databases, maps, and scripts over time, maintain rigor in details such as fields, coordinate systems, topology, and versions, and repeatedly check against requirements, this occupation's daily demands may be closer to your working style.

Reasons for caution | O*NET also shows for 15-1299.02: importance of being exact or highly accurate: 69% extremely important and 27% very important; prolonged sitting: 78% continually or almost continually; environmentally controlled indoor work: 89% daily; repeating the same tasks: 27% extremely important and 19% important; freedom to make decisions: 32% some freedom and 13% limited freedom; determining tasks, priorities, and goals: 34% a lot of freedom; time pressure: 47% monthly or more but not weekly; decision frequency: 26% monthly or more but not weekly; and repetitive motions: 30% continually or almost continually. This occupation works with geospatial data, databases, maps, and systems. A single wrong judgment about coordinate systems, projections, or field dictionaries, an undetected topology or geometry error, missing versions or metadata, or improper external transmission of controlled data or personal information may make outputs unusable and affect decisions and compliance. U.S. wages and employment cover parent group 15-1299, Computer Occupations, All Other; O*NET does not report separate exact figures for this occupation, and this page labels that coverage accurately. If sustained screen work and data detail are difficult for you, you struggle with frequent changes in requirements and data definitions, or you are unwilling to take responsibility for data quality and compliance, weigh these practical demands carefully.

Observation suggestion | Complete this page's G1 and recalculate 500m, 5cm, the duplicate-key excess of 200 people, and 4/16 minutes. Record how you retained UNKNOWN, actual times, and pending confirmations in this exercise. A single paper exercise does not demonstrate real GIS skills, long-term fit, or authorization.

Direct answer | This page's occupation corresponds to U.S. SOC 15-1299.02, Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians, labeled Bright Outlook by O*NET. Work falls into several categories: (one) data review and loading—review existing or incoming data for currency, accuracy, usefulness, quality, and documentation completeness, and enter data using coordinate geometry, keyboard entry, manual digitizing, scanning, or automatic vectorization; (two) spatial analysis and outputs—produce data layers, maps, tables, or reports using spatial analysis procedures or GIS technology, equipment, and systems, and perform integrated or computerized analyses to solve scientific problems; (three) database maintenance and development—maintain or modify existing GIS databases, design or coordinate integrated spatial or nonspatial GIS database development, and locate and integrate remote sensing or cartographic data; (four) cartography and visualization—select cartographic elements needed to present information effectively, design and prepare graphical representations of data, and create visualizations using analytical modeling, three-dimensional rendering, or cartographic output; (five) user support and consultation—provide GIS expertise and technical support to clients or users, discuss with users to analyze, configure, or troubleshoot applications, and prepare training materials or demonstrations; and (six) scripts and custom applications—conduct research, data analysis, system design, or support for GIS or GPS mapping software, and write, design, code, or test models, internet mapping solutions, or other applications. The work cycle connects requirements and data definition confirmation—data review and loading—coordinate, projection, topology, and field quality checks—spatial analysis and cartography—delivery of outputs, databases, and metadata—user support and review. This page distinguishes this occupation from adjacent geographers, cartographers and photogrammetrists, surveying and mapping technicians, computer systems analysts, and database administrators, and does not expand technical responsibilities to replace engineering, legal, or safety conclusions.

Standards and quality boundaries | Register sources, years, coordinates, fields, versions, check results, and limitations. Articles 27—29 of China's Surveying and Mapping Law set qualifications and scope for surveying and mapping entities; Articles 30—31 address personnel practice conditions and work credentials. Do not equate all GIS processing with credentialed surveying and mapping. Article 34 requires prescribed approval for external provision of surveying and mapping results constituting state secrets; Article 37 concerns review and publication of important geographic information; Article 39 requires quality accountability. These do not imply administrative approval for all ordinary data sharing. Apply Articles PIPL4/6/13/19 according to identifiable natural persons, lawful basis, minimum necessity, and retention period; anonymized information is not personal information. Separately check the applicability of system security, cross-border, and other rules to actual systems and data; they are not a uniform occupational license.

Boundary conclusion | This page corresponds to U.S. SOC 15-1299.02. The main differences from adjacent roles are their focus, outputs, and authorization level. This occupation works with geospatial data, databases, maps, and systems support, producing datasets, layers, maps, reports, and application support. Geographers (19-3092.00) research and explain regional and spatial phenomena, producing research findings and explanations. Cartographers and photogrammetrists (17-1021.00) focus on map design, image processing, and photogrammetric solutions, producing maps and imagery. Surveying and mapping technicians focus on surveying operations, records, and mapping support, producing surveying and mapping records. Computer systems analysts (15-1211.00) focus on business processes, system requirements analysis, and solution design, producing system requirements and solutions. Database administrators (15-1242.00) focus on databases, permissions, backups, and performance, producing database operation and security records. Their focus and authorization levels differ; authority for engineering or safety conclusions or production system changes cannot be carried over between roles.

Core principles of adjacent roles | Most roles in the same group or nearby aim to support understanding and decisions with verifiable data and systems. They differ in focus, outputs, and authorization level: some work with geospatial data, databases, maps, and application support; others with research and explanations of regional and spatial phenomena; others with maps, imagery, and photogrammetry; others with surveying operations and records; others with business processes and system requirements; and others with database operations and security.

This occupation's core purpose | Work with geospatial data, databases, maps, and application support within data, compliance, and authorization requirements: review and load data according to requirements and data definitions; check coordinates, projections, topology, and fields; perform spatial analysis, statistics, and cartography; maintain and develop databases and applications; provide user support and training; and deliver and apply outputs within authorization. Data and outputs must be verifiable, definitions and versions traceable, and boundaries explainable.

Primary subjects and bases in adjacent roles | Geographers rely on research questions, methods, data sources, and interpretation requirements; cartographers and photogrammetrists on map design standards, image processing, and photogrammetric solution requirements; surveying and mapping technicians on surveying standards, instruments, and record requirements; computer systems analysts on business processes, system requirements, and solution design methods; and database administrators on database management, permissions, backups, performance, and security requirements.

This occupation's primary subjects and bases | Work concerns geospatial data sources, years, boundaries, coordinate systems, projections, accuracy, field dictionaries, topology, geometry, metadata, versions, layers, maps, reports, applications, and user support. It follows geographic information, data quality, metadata, and cartographic standards; data disclosure, confidentiality, personal information, cross-border data transfer, and cybersecurity requirements; and surveying, mapping, and geographic information authority rules.

Career profile | This occupation corresponds to U.S. SOC 15-1299.02, Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians, updated by O*NET in 2026 and labeled Bright Outlook. Practitioners perform geospatial data and systems technical work in government, professional, scientific, and technical services, information, engineering, consulting, planning, and other settings. They review and load geospatial data; produce data layers, maps, tables, or reports using spatial analysis procedures or GIS technology and equipment; maintain and modify GIS databases and design or coordinate integrated database development; select cartographic elements and design and prepare graphical representations and three-dimensional visualizations; provide clients or users technical expertise, support, and training; and work on GIS or GPS mapping software. O*NET details show the 2024 industry distribution for parent group 15-1299: professional, scientific, and technical services 27%, government 23%, and other industries, including information and finance and insurance, 50%. The 50% is a category in the original table; the three categories total 100%. These are neither separate GIS figures nor 2025 data. The work environment mainly involves office screen work, prolonged sitting, and accuracy demands.

Core processes in adjacent roles | Geographers focus on problem definition, data compilation, analysis, and explanation; cartographers and photogrammetrists on image processing, photogrammetric solutions, and map design; surveying and mapping technicians on surveying operations, instrument use, documentation, and mapping support; computer systems analysts on requirements research, process analysis, and solution design; and database administrators on database deployment, permissions, backups, performance, and troubleshooting.

This occupation's core process | Confirm requirements and data definitions; review data, register sources, and load; check coordinates, projections, topology, and fields; perform spatial analysis, statistics, and cartography; prepare outputs, databases, metadata, and explanations; and review, deliver, and support users. Every step must leave a trace according to data, quality, and security procedures and be reviewable by supervisors and peers.

Main outputs in adjacent roles | Geographers produce research or analytical findings and explanations; cartographers and photogrammetrists produce maps, imagery, and photogrammetric reports; surveying and mapping technicians produce surveying, setting-out, and mapping records; computer systems analysts produce system requirements, solutions, and process descriptions; and database administrators produce database operation, permissions, backup, and performance records.

This occupation's main outputs | Verifiable data processing and loading records and metadata; spatial analysis and statistical results; data layers, maps, charts, reports, and three-dimensional visualizations; GIS databases, applications, and internet mapping solutions; user support and training materials; and review and delivery records.

Responsible parties in adjacent roles | Responsibilities in the same group and adjacent roles are usually defined by the institution, standards, and authorization, and commonly concern projects, clients, users, data security, and system stability.

Responsible parties in this occupation | Practitioners are responsible for their own data processing, loading, quality checks, outputs, databases, and support records, and for checks and reviews meeting coordinate, topology, field, version, and reproducibility requirements. Use and external provision of controlled data, classified data, and personal information; production system changes, deployment, and account permissions; and engineering, safety, or legal conclusions are decided under institutional procedures by appropriately authorized roles or institutions. This occupation does not replace those decisions.

Permissions and approvals in adjacent roles | Authority in the same group and adjacent roles derives from institutional authorization, standards, and procedures. It usually does not include independent decisions on data provision, system changes, or publication of conclusions beyond one's authorization or scope. Matters involving personal information, controlled data, production systems, or safety should be transferred to the relevant roles or institutions.

Permissions and approvals in this occupation | External publication, provision, and deployment of data, maps, and applications must remain within institutional and project authorization and data disclosure, confidentiality, and personal information requirements. Collection, sharing, and cross-border transfer of controlled or classified data; production changes, accounts, permissions, and data deletion; and use of conclusions for engineering, safety, or decision-making require approval from or transfer to the relevant roles or institutions under procedures. Do not publish or make changes without authority.

Conclusion boundaries in adjacent roles | Conclusions in the same group and adjacent roles are usually limited to the project, standards, and responsibilities concerned. They generally do not determine engineering safety, legal liability, or formal appraisal conclusions. Cross-disciplinary application and use for legal or safety purposes have scope limitations.

This occupation's conclusion boundaries | Technical conclusions state only verifiable sources, coordinates, fields, topology, processing steps, results, and limitations, distinguishing compliance with accuracy and standards from out-of-limit findings and pending review. Do not make unauthorized judgments or promises about matters beyond your authority, such as engineering or safety conclusions, controlled data provision, or major production system changes. Pause and escalate or transfer coordinate system conflicts, topology errors, misleading results, or suspected data leaks. Definitions must also withstand review by supervisors, peers, data management staff, and competent authorities.

Pre-employment checking | Use the following six items to check details before applying or starting work, rather than inferring duties and authority from titles or promotional wording. Base findings on written job postings, employment contracts, role descriptions, and data and security procedures, and continue confirming after starting. This page lists checking directions, not a formal institutional or project requirements checklist. In particular, this occupation often involves controlled data, personal information, production systems, and account permissions. Confirm specific requirements for data access, use, publication, deployment, and confidentiality.

Checking points | Similar titles can involve very different duties and authority. Some roles focus on data loading, quality checks, and cartography; others on spatial analysis and modeling; database and platform operations; application and script development; user support and training; or project management and consulting. Authorization for data access, use, publication, deployment, and confidentiality also varies by institution and jurisdiction.

01 Actual duties and authorization boundaries | Check whether the role independently handles data processing, analysis, mapping, and system changes or mainly assists with entry and cartography. Check accessible and usable data scope and definitions; permitted software, platforms, computing resources, and account permissions; authority to process controlled data and personal information; approval requirements for external publication or deployment; and collaboration and responsibility routing with geographic information, business, and security teams.

Checking points | This occupation often involves production systems, account permissions, controlled data, personal information, and prolonged screen work. It commonly requires data and security training, account and device management requirements, and eye-care, ergonomic, and occupational health guidance.

This table makes no numerical comparison and does not use one occupation's wages as a proxy for another. Introduction | The comparison uses four columns: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which choice may fit better. Geographic information, geographic research, cartography, surveying, systems analysis, and databases often connect within one project or institution, but connection does not mean interchangeability. When moving between directions, learn that direction's data definitions, methods, authorization, and responsibility boundaries anew.

Key differences: GIS emphasizes spatial data, databases, applications, analysis, and user support. Geography emphasizes research and explanation of spatial phenomena; cartography and photogrammetry emphasize maps and imagery; surveying technicians emphasize surveying and mapping support; systems analysis and DBA work emphasize system solutions and database operations. Tasks overlap. Occupational titles cannot rule out others' responsibility across the full process; authority follows actual role arrangements.

May better suit people willing to work with geospatial data, databases, maps, and scripts over time, maintain rigor in details such as fields, coordinate systems, topology, and versions, and repeatedly check against requirements.

Outputs include datasets, layers, maps, reports, databases, and application support (U.S. SOC 15-1299.02).

Key difference: Geographers emphasize research and explanation of regional phenomena and may also maintain GIS. This occupation's core includes GIS analysis of scientific problems and research/system design support. Both may conduct research; do not conclude that GIS generally has no research responsibility.

May better suit people who want to define research questions, compile data, analyze, and explain. This occupation places more emphasis on data processing, loading, quality checks, cartography, and systems support.

Core work and outputs: Collect and compile geographic data from censuses, field observations, satellite imagery, aerial photographs, existing maps, and other sources; analyze distributions of physical and human phenomena at multiple scales and study regional population characteristics; use geographic information software and cartographic principles to create and modify maps; and write and present research reports. Geographic information systems technologists and technicians | Produce verifiable datasets, layers, maps, reports, databases, and application support: review and load geospatial data, produce outputs using spatial analysis or GIS, maintain and develop databases and applications, and support users (U.S. SOC 15-1299.02).

What personality is better suited to geographic information systems technology work? The occupation places greater weight on rigor in data, definitions, and versions; ongoing learning of technologies and tools; the ability to translate requirements into checkable plans; and willingness to take responsibility for data compliance and output quality, rather than a particular personality type. O*NET lists CIR (Conventional—Investigative—Realistic), with work styles emphasizing intellectual curiosity, attention to detail, and dependability. These can be starting points for exploration.

Can introverts do this work? Yes. It includes substantial independent data processing, scripting, and documentation, alongside communication with data providers, business teams, and users: email 35% daily; telephone communication 47% weekly or more but not daily; face-to-face or individual and team discussions 33% daily and 40% weekly or more but not daily.
Extroversion is not an entry requirement. This page has not verified that extroversion improves GIS communication or performance. Observe actual explanations of requirements and reviews.

Which MBTI type is best for this occupation? No type has been shown to be best. MBTI is not a professional qualification or ability assessment tool. Career adjustment mainly depends on awareness of data and methods, standards compliance, and software, database, and security abilities.

Which Holland interest types are more relevant to this occupation? O*NET lists CIR: Conventional (organizing information and data and maintaining accurate records according to standards and procedures), Investigative (analyzing and researching data problems), and Realistic (operating equipment and software and handling practical objects). Use this to explore task preferences, not predict performance.
This page has not obtained occupation-specific validation of personality prediction. Unverified group trends cannot be treated as individual evidence.

Can someone who struggles with math do this work? Quantitative skills involving coordinates, geometry, statistics, and data processing are needed, and daily work involves data, fields, and scripts. Quantitative foundations can be developed through training, but complete difficulty with data and quantitative work creates substantial limitations.
Collaboration follows the actual role, without a specific emotional intelligence score requirement. This page has not verified that high emotional intelligence improves outcomes.

Can the Enneagram determine whether I am suited to this work? No. It is a self-exploration tool, not a conclusion about occupational ability or fit. Evaluate whether you can complete loading, quality checks, analysis, and delivery under data and standards requirements.

paragraphs: Boundaries | These are task-based failure scenarios and editorial control suggestions; no incidence rates or severity rankings have been established. Check handling and change requirements against actual data classification, systems, jurisdiction, project, and authorization. Not all GIS processing involves credentialed surveying and mapping, competent authority approval, or the same cross-border process. Transfer anomalies to the actual responsible role.

Risk examples include conflicting data definitions, coordinates, or fields; uncontrolled factual records and versions; unauthorized information provision or production system operations; and collaboration or outsourcing interruptions. These are not frequency or severity rankings. First check data, testing, review, and permissions. Pause the affected step when anomalies arise and obtain evidence and transfer matters according to actual procedures.

Evidence scope | This page summarizes O*NET 15-1299.02 tasks and work context: review data currency, accuracy, usefulness, and quality 82; produce layers, maps, tables, or reports using spatial analysis or GIS 81; maintain or modify existing databases 78; select cartographic elements 71; enter data 68; interpret aerial or orthophoto imagery 67; use specialized software to create, analyze, report, or convert data 66; design, program, or model applications or procedures 64; advanced spatial analysis and modeling 64; meet clients to discuss technical specifications 63; work with computers 86; get information 85; process information 82; analyze data or information 81; identify objects, actions, and events 80; environmentally controlled indoor work 89% daily; prolonged sitting 78% continually or almost continually; importance of being exact or highly accurate 69% extremely important and 27% very important; repeating the same tasks 27% extremely important; time pressure 47% monthly or more but not weekly. Data, output, and security requirements reference data protection, surveying and mapping results, cybersecurity, and personal information management rules. Wage and employment figures cover parent occupational group 15-1299 and provide background only, not risk assessment inputs.
The practitioner, data staff, and project staff; clients, users, and decision-makers

Wrong judgments about data years, administrative boundaries, coordinate systems, projections, or field dictionaries; combining or overlaying data with incomparable definitions; undetected topology or geometry errors; or missing, untraceable metadata may cause systematic output errors and affect engineering, planning, and business decisions.

Before work, check data sources, years, boundaries, coordinates, and fields and record the basis. Validate processing and mapping according to standards and reproducibility requirements, retaining scripts and intermediate results. Immediately pause for review and rework when definitions conflict, coordinate systems, topology, or fields are wrong, or results are abnormal.

Scenario | The regional boundaries and statistical data supplied for a project use inconsistent definitions. Under a tight deadline, the requester wants maps and conclusions produced from existing data first and verified later.
The practitioner, data staff, and quality staff; the institution, users, and auditors

Missing original data, script parameters, or versions; fabrication, backdating, or untraceable rewrites; and outputs inconsistent with databases may affect reproduction and audits. Lawful corrections are not fabrication.

Retain original values and versions, stating reasons, responsible people, and actual correction times. Mark unverified fields UNKNOWN and request review; do not backdate or fabricate supplements from templates.

Scenario | During handover, you find the previous shift's analysis script lacks parameter and data version records and that result layers do not match the database version. Someone suggests filling the gaps from a template.
The practitioner, data staff, and security staff; the institution, clients, and data subjects

Failure to manage controlled data, classified data, or personal information according to minimum necessity, approval, and confidentiality requirements, or unauthorized external publication, provision, or cross-border transfer, may violate data protection, surveying and mapping results, and cybersecurity requirements and cause legal and security consequences.

Handle identifiable personal information according to lawful basis, minimum necessity, permissions, and retention periods. Do not provide it in uncontrolled group chats without authorization; use permitted channels to ask security/data staff to check. Competent authority approval applies only where actual legal provisions require it.
Scenario | A party requests data containing personal information or controlled geographic information in an uncontrolled group chat for quick coordination.
The practitioner, operations staff, and security staff; the institution, users, and orderly production operations

Unauthorized production changes, data deletion, or permission adjustments, or issuing engineering, safety, or compliance conclusions in place of authorized roles, may cause system failures, data loss, and legal and reputational risks.

Follow change, approval, testing, and rollback procedures for production changes and permission adjustments. Transfer engineering, safety, and compliance conclusions to the relevant roles or institutions. When asked to exceed authority, first explain the boundary and transfer through the required process.
Scenario | During a staffing shortage, you are asked to change the production database or delete data directly, skipping testing and approval to deploy that day.
The practitioner, team, and platform staff; project progress and system availability

Key data, scripts, or system permissions depend on one person, so resignation, sick leave, account expiration, or device failure interrupts processing and delivery. This may delay projects and affect system availability and output continuity.

Establish backup and handover rules for scripts, configurations, permissions, documentation, and personnel. Keep key processes and parameters reproducible and traceable. Escalate staffing, permission, or resource shortages according to procedures and adjust priorities; do not deploy with unresolved hazards.

Scenario | The only colleague familiar with a data workflow and system configuration is on leave. The project is asked to have that colleague guide by telephone while untrained staff temporarily process and publish results.
The practitioner, contractors, and technical service providers; the project, outputs, and data security

Unclear delivery and acceptance for outsourced data collection, development, or platform services, or unclear ownership of data, outputs, and code and fee changes, may cause rework, fee disputes, and unclear quality and data security accountability.

For outsourcing and technical collaboration, define and record scope, standards, acceptance, data and output ownership, and fee change rules. Review and accept deliverables. Pause for review and escalation when delivery, acceptance, or ownership disputes arise.

Scenario | After development or data processing, a contractor requests payment without submitting source code, test records, or acceptance records. You are asked to sign off first and obtain the missing items later.

values: M1 | Entirely fictional G1, v1, year 2025. A 60-minute paper/pen/calculator exercise with no real region, residents, or system. Layer L contains A(0,0), B(300,400), and C(600,0), in m, using the same stipulated local plane with X east and Y north, unrelated to any national CRS. Statistical layer T gives A a population of 100 and B a population of 200; C has no row. Area keys are case-sensitive and must be unique. Calculate paper distances at 1:10000 and distances from O to the points, where O(0,0). The closed buffer threshold is 500m (≤ included), not travel distance or service coverage.

M2 | Received table J-v1 has three rows: A/100, B/200, and B/200. Statistics also cover 2025, and population is measured in people. entries.answer: The main differences concern focus, outputs, and authorization level. This occupation works with geospatial data, databases, maps, and systems support, producing datasets, layers, maps, reports, and application support. Geographers (19-3092.00) research and explain regional and spatial phenomena; cartographers and photogrammetrists (17-1021.00) focus on map design, image processing, and photogrammetric solutions; surveying and mapping technicians on surveying operations, records, and mapping support; computer systems analysts (15-1211.00) on business processes, system requirements analysis, and solution design; and database administrators (15-1242.00) on databases, permissions, backups, and performance. subject.name: Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians
subject.summary: This occupation corresponds to U.S. O*NET/SOC 15-1299.02, Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians (the fixed Chinese index name translates as Information Systems Technologists and Technicians). They assist scientists or related professionals in building, maintaining, modifying, or using geographic information systems (GIS) databases, and may also perform some custom application development or provide user support. Core work includes reviewing existing or incoming data for currency, accuracy, usefulness, quality, and documentation completeness; producing data layers, maps, tables, or reports using spatial analysis procedures or GIS technology and equipment; maintaining or modifying existing GIS databases; selecting cartographic elements and designing and preparing graphical representations and three-dimensional visualizations of data; entering data into databases and interpreting aerial or orthophoto imagery; using specialized application software to create, analyze, report, or convert data; designing, programming, or modeling GIS applications or procedures; and providing clients or users with technical expertise, support, and training. Official scope: Assist scientists or related professionals in building, maintaining, modifying, or using geographic information systems (GIS) databases. Wage and employment coverage: The figures O*NET displays under this occupation are labeled as covering the parent occupational group 15-1299, Computer Occupations, All Other.
